request_debug.prompt_preview:
You write per-candidate post-mortems for a slopmortem pipeline. Given a fresh pitch and one dead-startup canonical document, produce a single LLMSynthesis JSON object that explains why this dead startup is similar, where the new pitch could diverge, what killed the dead startup, and what the new founder should learn.

Rules:
- Ground every claim in the candidate document or in tool calls. Do not invent facts.
- A `Trusted facts` block (typed pipeline data — not user input) appears below the pitc

response.text: {"candidate_id":"ubiome::biotech","name":"ubiome","one_liner":"US-based consumer microbiome sequencing startup (mail-in kit + app) that collapsed in 2019 after an FBI raid over Medicare insurance fraud and subsequent SEC charges against its founders.","similarity":{"business_model":{"score":4,"rationale":"Both use a recurring/subscription monetization model targeting consumers and bundle a digital app layer with a health data product. However, uBiome's core was a physical mail-in diagnostic kit with lab sequencing; the new pitch is a pure digital subscription (symptom tracking + telehealth), with no physical product or lab component."},"market":{"score":3,"rationale":"Both operate in consumer healthtech with a focus on personal health data and chronic/ongoing health conditions. uBiome was US-only and focused on microbiome sequencing; the new pitch targets chronic-illness patients in Germany and France, a distinct geography and condition-agnostic digital-health market with different regulatory regimes (EU MDR, GDPR, German DiGA framework)."},"gtm":{"score":3,"rationale":"uBiome used crowdfunding, citizen-science framing, and Y Combinator/VC backing to reach early adopters. The new pitch's GTM is unspecified in the trusted facts, but its B2C subscription model suggests direct-to-consumer digital channels rather than the crowdfunding/citizen-science approach uBiome used. Geography (EU vs US) also implies entirely different payer and distribution dynamics."},"stage_scale":{"score":4,"rationale":"Both are early-stage consumer health startups with a subscription model seeking to build a recurring user base. uBiome reached a $600M valuation before collapse, suggesting significant scale; the new pitch's stage is unknown per trusted facts, likely earlier."}},"why_similar":"Both are consumer-facing healthtech plays that wrap health data collection in a recurring subscription and a companion app, targeting individuals who want ongoing insight into their health. uBiome similarly combined a consumer app with a health-monitoring product and used subscription monetization — the structural DNA of the new pitch mirrors this pattern. Both also face the inherent tension of consumer health data products sitting at the boundary between wellness and regulated medical diagnostics.","where_diverged":"Several concrete dimensions differ: (1) Geography — uBiome operated in the US and navigated Medicare/FDA; the new pitch operates in Germany and France under EU regulations (DiGA digital health app framework, EU MDR, GDPR), creating a fundamentally different regulatory and reimbursement environment. (2) Product type — uBiome's product was a physical mail-in lab-sequencing kit; the new pitch is entirely digital (symptom tracking + telehealth), eliminating lab-processing risk and insurance billing complexity. (3) Sub-sector — uBiome was specifically microbiome sequencing (genomics/biotech); the new pitch is a general chronic-illness management and telehealth platform, not tied to any single diagnostic modality. (4) Monetization risk — uBiome's collapse was driven by fraudulent insurance billing to Medicare; the new pitch's direct-to-consumer monthly subscription model avoids third-party payer billing entirely, removing that specific fraud vector.","failure_causes":["Medicare/insurance fraud via unauthorized and repeated patient billing","FBI raid triggering operational shutdown and loss of stakeholder trust","SEC charges against founders for $60M investor fraud","Founders charged with conspiracy to commit fraud and money laundering","Founders becoming fugitives, destroying any path to company survival","Ethical lapses in citizen-science data collection and informed consent","Aggressive growth tactics that prioritized billing revenue over patient and doctor trust"],"lessons_for_input":["Design your billing and subscription flows with airtight patient consent records — fraudulent or unauthorized charges are an existential risk in consumer health.","Engage the relevant regulatory bodies early (German DiGA, French HAS, GDPR authorities) rather than treating compliance as a post-launch concern.","Keep founder conduct and governance structures clean and auditable from day one; investor and regulatory trust is destroyed permanently by fraud allegations.","Build clinical and ethical credibility (IRB equivalents, data governance) before scaling, especially when handling sensitive chronic-illness patient data.","Avoid over-reliance on insurance or third-party reimbursement schemes for revenue; your direct-subscription model is a strength — protect it by keeping the consumer relationship transparent."]}
